paras: The police shooting of Sam Duckett took place on Christmas afternoon, 25 December 1881, in South Washington, D.C., when Officer Branson shot Duckett, a Black man, in the head during a street fight over the arrest of his sister, Ellen Duckett. Duckett survived, was arrested three days later, pleaded guilty in Police Court and was fined $10 or thirty days. Washington's daily papers told the story as an attack on two policemen by a Black crowd.

The fight began a little after 3 o'clock on Sunday afternoon in a neighborhood the Evening Star called "Fredericksburg" and the National Republican called "the Island"; the Evening Critic described it as "the lowest and most degraded district of the city." Officer Howell tried to arrest Ellen Duckett, whom the Star accused of being disorderly and blowing a tin horn, at 3d and M streets southwest, or Third and L by the Republican's account.

According to the Star, at least fifteen hundred people, "most of them colored," gathered within minutes, and men and women attacked the officers with sticks and stones for half an hour. The Star said Sam Duckett struck Branson in the breast with a large stone and was reaching for another when the officer fired. In the Republican's version Duckett led the crowd in an effort to rescue his sister, and Branson, struck by stones, thrown down and stripped of his club, badge and belt, drew his pistol and "saw a man drop to the ground face downwards." The Critic's account had Duckett, a rock in each hand, throw a stone that wounded Howell on the head as Howell's small pistol went off, and Branson then fired as Duckett stooped for a second rock. The German-language Washingtoner Journal gave a different order: Duckett attacked Branson, who shot him through the head after trying to shake him off, and only then did friends of the family attack the officers.

Branson went to help Howell, who was cut and bitten, and the two officers took Ellen Duckett to the station house after a mounted relief arrived. When Branson returned he found only a pool of blood, and the Evening Critic reported that four or five of the crowd had carried Duckett off, supposedly over the James Creek bridge to his mother's. Accounts of the wound differed, from the Republican's first guess of the right side near the heart to later reports that the ball entered the back of the head and came out at the forehead.

On 26 December Ellen Duckett was sentenced to eleven months and twenty-nine days in jail for assaulting Howell, and two others from the crowd, Sam Berry and Agnes Ware, were fined. The Republican reported that twelve participants had been arrested. Sergeant Mulhall and Officers Howe and Gibson arrested Sam Duckett about 11 o'clock on Wednesday night, 28 December, in a shanty near Sixteenth street and Georgia avenue southeast.

Represented by H. H. Wells Jr., Duckett had his case continued and then, on 31 December, pleaded guilty in Police Court. The court fined him $10 or thirty days, saying it took into account "the suffering he has undergone from the pistol-shot wound." No report of any inquiry into Branson's use of his pistol appears in the coverage.

Coverage came from Washington's own papers between 26 and 31 December: the Star, the Critic, the National Republican and the German-language Washingtoner Journal. Every account came from the officers' side, and none gave a version from Duckett or the crowd, though they disagreed on whom Duckett attacked and when the crowd joined in. The Critic headlined "Two Officers Assaulted by a Negro Mob" and called Ellen Duckett "the wench," while the Star called Sam Duckett "a desperate character" and the Republican "a notorious thief and rowdy."

The Critic went further on 27 December, calling Duckett "a vicious rascal" and writing that if he died "the community would not be very much distressed." The Washingtoner Journal headlined a "bloody fight between policemen and Negroes" and headed its report of Ellen Duckett's sentence "Gerechte Strafe," or just punishment. The Star headed its report of the light sentence "Let him off easy because he was shot in the head."

The Star and Republican told the story from the officers' side, calling Duckett 'a desperate character' and 'a notorious thief and rowdy' and the crowd 'roughs'.

The German-language Washingtoner Journal headlined a 'bloody fight between policemen and Negroes', praised the officers' 'brave resistance', and headed Ellen Duckett's sentence 'Gerechte Strafe' (Just punishment).
